issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette:
Rajan Mehta is a 53-year-old South Asian man who works as a painter - not the trade kind, but an artist, a man who has spent the better part of three decades rendering light and landscape in oils. He is married, the father of two adult children, and lives in a mid-sized city in the American Midwest. He came to the clinic quietly, almost apologetically, as though uncertain he had earned the right to be there.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Rajan was visiting extended family in a region of South Asia experiencing escalating civil conflict. He had made the trip many times before and had not anticipated danger. On his third day there, the neighborhood where he was staying came under shelling. He was inside a relative's home when an explosion struck a building across the street. The blast shattered windows, filled the room with a choking smell of smoke, burning plastic, and something metallic he could not name, and threw him to the floor. He lay there for what felt like a very long time, unable to move, unable to determine whether the structure around him was stable, whether more shells were coming, whether the people in the next room were alive. The helplessness of those minutes - the absolute absence of any action he could take, the world entirely beyond his reach - lodged itself somewhere beneath the level of conscious memory.

He returned to the United States physically unharmed. For the first few weeks, he told himself he was fine. He went back to his studio, stood before a blank canvas, and found that something had gone quiet in him. He began to notice that when a car backfired on the street outside, his body responded before his mind did - a violent flinch, a surge of readiness that had nowhere to go, his muscles braced for impact. He started keeping the studio windows closed, and then started spending less time there altogether. He told his wife he was simply tired.

The smell of certain things became difficult: smoke from a neighbor's fireplace, the particular chemical odor of some oil paints he had used for years. He could not always say why he moved away from these things quickly, only that he did. At the same time, he found himself going over and over the event in his mind - not to relive it exactly, but to understand it, to locate some reason why it had happened to him, some logic that would make it fit into the shape of his life. The questions circled without resolution. He began filling his hours with tasks: home repairs, administrative errands, anything that required his hands and foreclosed the space in which the questions arose. He stopped reading the news entirely, deleting apps from his phone after a headline about renewed shelling in the region left him unable to sleep for two nights.

What troubled him most, perhaps, was what happened to his painting. He had always understood himself through his work - the capacity to see, to render, to make something that communicated feeling across distance. When memories of the event surfaced in the studio, he would notice his body curling slightly, shoulders rounding, as though he were back on that floor. With the memory came a grief so heavy it felt physical, and alongside it a disorienting sense that the event could not really have happened to him - that it belonged to some other story, some other man. He had come to believe that whatever had made him a painter was no longer available to him. His wife had noticed the unfinished canvases accumulating. She had stopped asking about them.

He remained constantly alert in ways he could not fully explain - scanning rooms when he entered them, tensing at sounds that others around him seemed not to register. His body felt perpetually coiled. He had begun to feel, with a quiet certainty that frightened him, that the world was simply not safe, that this had always been true and he had simply not known it.

What finally brought him to the clinic was his wife sitting across from him at dinner and asking, gently, where he had gone. He did not have an answer. What he most hoped for, he said in the intake session, was to want to paint again. What he most feared was that the man who had painted was gone for good.
